node-1.label: Since 2014, recurrent abscesses, indurated erythematous plaques, and sclerosis on both upper legs

node-2.label: 56-year-old woman with medical history of hypermobility syndrome diagnosed in 1998 and cosmetic breast augmentation surgery in 2002

node-3.label: Progressive chronic fatigue and joint pain over years without definitive diagnosis despite multiple specialist consultations; no symptoms of autoinflammation or autoimmunity besides periodic fever

node-4.label: Physical examination revealed indurated erythematous plaques, sclerosis, and abscesses on both upper legs; no other significant physical findings noted

why.why: The newly identified histiocytic MORO-positive particles in the biopsy further support a chronic bacterial infection, and both the laboratory and pathology experts independently favor an infectious/immunodeficiency etiology over autoimmune, neoplastic, and sarcoidotic alternatives. The recurrent abscesses, indurated plaques, and granulomatous/lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with fibrosis are all consistent with this. Confidence is raised from 0.70 to 0.75, but remains short of definitive because wound culture, special stains, and immunologic workup are still pending.

The laboratory and pathology experts both interpret the biopsy pattern as arguing against autoimmune/autoinflammatory dermatosis, and clinically there is no systemic autoinflammation/autoimmunity beyond periodic fever. These expert analyses further reduce the already low likelihood.

Both experts exclude cutaneous neoplasm/lymphoproliferative disease on histology, which shows granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis without neoplastic features. With no supporting evidence for malignancy, confidence is lowered.

node-8.label: Skin biopsy shows granulomatous and lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, septal/fascial sclerosis, and histiocytic fibrosis

why.why: Although granulomatous histology and systemic symptoms could suggest sarcoidosis, both experts emphasize that recurrent abscesses make sarcoidosis less likely than an infectious/immunodeficiency etiology. The absence of broader autoimmunity also weighs against it, so confidence is lowered.

node-10.label: Recurrent bacterial skin abscesses (Staphylococcus aureus infection)

why.why: The pathologist’s identification of histiocytic MORO-positive particles adds histologic support for chronic bacterial infection, and both experts identify recurrent bacterial skin abscesses, most plausibly Staphylococcus aureus, as the leading diagnosis. The granulomatous and lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with fibrosis is compatible with this. Confidence is increased from 0.55 to 0.65, but confirmatory wound culture and special stains are still unavailable.

attrs.why: The chronic course since 2014, recurrent abscess-like lesions, indurated plaques, and biopsy findings of granulomatous inflammation with histiocytic fibrosis are characteristic of atypical mycobacterial skin infection. This refines the infectious/immunodeficiency frontier by specifying a chronic granulomatous infectious etiology that explains both the histopathology and the indolent clinical presentation.

why.why: The experts note that immunologic evaluation (immunoglobulins, lymphocyte subsets, neutrophil function) has not been performed, leaving an underlying immunodeficiency as a viable explanation for recurrent abscesses and chronic infection-like histology. Confidence is modestly increased from 0.20 to 0.25 pending these tests.

attrs.why: Granulomatous and histiocytic inflammation with fibrosis and recurrent abscess-like cutaneous lesions can also be seen in deep fungal infections, especially in an indolent chronic presentation. Although less common than bacterial or mycobacterial causes, this remains a plausible subcategory of the infectious frontier and warrants consideration given the biopsy findings.
